buildings.name: Circus Flaminius (open field)
buildings.summary: Laid out by the censor Gaius Flaminius in 221 BC on the Prata Flaminia: not a racecourse with stands but a long open space used for the plebeian games, for assemblies, for triumphal musters and as the start of the triumphal procession. Victory temples and porticoes lined its edges.

phases.t: laid out by the censor C. Flaminius
triumphal games and temples begin to line it

scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 83
Gatti, in Carettoni et al., La pianta marmorea di Roma antica (1960)
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project (formaurbis.stanford.edu), fr. 31ii
Coarelli, Il Campo Marzio dalle origini alla fine della repubblica (1997)
buildings.note: Following Gatti: an open strip about 300 x 100 m between the Tiber and the joint facade of the Porticus Octaviae and Porticus Philippi, running ESE-WNW parallel to that facade, with its rounded end to the WNW under Monte dei Cenci. rot 124 = from the rounded WNW end toward the open ESE end (the schema's circus convention). Boundaries on the long sides are the Marble Plan lines (fr. 31ii, 31u, 31cc, 31z); length is reasoned from Monte dei Cenci to the Theatre of Marcellus. No seating has ever been found.

buildings.name: Circus Flaminius (paved piazza)
buildings.summary: After the Augustan rebuilding of the Porticus Octaviae and Philippi and the building of the Theatre of Marcellus, which cut into its eastern end, the Circus Flaminius was a monumental paved piazza in front of the porticoes. In 2 BC it was flooded and 36 crocodiles were slaughtered in it. The Regionary Catalogues still name it in the 4th century.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 83
Gatti, in Carettoni et al., La pianta marmorea di Roma antica (1960)
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project (formaurbis.stanford.edu), fr. 31ii
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Circus Flaminius
buildings.note: Gatti suggested the area was paved in the imperial period. Same footprint as v1; the Theatre of Marcellus overlaps its ESE end.

buildings.name: Temple of Apollo Medicus
buildings.summary: Vowed in 433 BC during a plague and dedicated by the consul Gnaeus Julius in 431, the first and for centuries the only temple of Apollo in Rome, outside the pomerium in the Prata Flaminia (the Apollinar). The Senate met here when it had to receive generals and envoys outside the city.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 12
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Apollo, aedes in circo
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
buildings.note: Form unknown: a tufa podium of an earlier temple was found under the Augustan one. Modelled as a small Tuscan temple on the later footprint and orientation; dimensions are guesses.

buildings.name: Temple of Apollo Medicus (restored 179 BC)
buildings.summary: Restored in the mid-Republican building campaigns; in 179 BC the censor M. Fulvius Nobilior contracted for a porticus running from the temple toward the Tiber. A podium wall attributed by Frank to this phase survives under the Augustan temple.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 12
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Apollo, aedes in circo
buildings.note: Frank dated much of the surviving podium to 179 BC; others (Delbrueck) to the original. Form conjectural.

buildings.name: Temple of Apollo Sosianus
buildings.summary: Rebuilt from 34 BC by Gaius Sosius, Antony's partisan, and completed after Actium as an Augustan monument, dedicated on 23 September, Augustus' birthday. Hexastyle, with Carrara marble columns along the front and pronaos and engaged columns down the cella; the pediment carried a Greek Amazonomachy of the 5th century BC and the cella held famous Greek statuary. Three columns stand re-erected beside the Theatre of Marcellus.

phases.t: dedicated on 23 September as an Augustan monument (date approximate)

scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 12-13
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Apollo, aedes in circo
La Rocca, Amazzonomachia: le sculture frontonali del tempio di Apollo Sosiano (1985)
buildings.note: Oriented almost due south, unlike its neighbours. The frontal stair was replaced by two lateral stairs when the Theatre of Marcellus was built against its front. Column height ~14.6 m from the re-erected columns; podium ~40 x 21 m.

buildings.name: Temple of Bellona
buildings.summary: Vowed by Appius Claudius Caecus in 296 BC during the battle against Etruscans and Samnites. Outside the pomerium, it was where the Senate received envoys and victorious generals asking for triumphs; before it stood the Columna Bellica, over which the fetial threw the spear that declared war on a distant enemy.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 57-58
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Bellona, aedes in circo
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
buildings.note: Identified (Coarelli) with the podium immediately east of Apollo Sosianus, which has a different orientation; rot 170 is approximate. Dedication date c. 290 BC assumed.

buildings.name: Temple of Bellona (Augustan restoration)
buildings.summary: Restored in the Augustan remodelling of the area around the Theatre of Marcellus, when Bellona, Apollo and the theatre were tied into one architectural group. Still the setting of the Senate's war ceremonies under the emperors; Marcus Aurelius threw the fetial spear from the Columna Bellica in 178.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 57-58
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
buildings.note: Augustan restoration inferred from the tight planning of the group; details conjectural.

buildings.name: Temple of Pietas (in circo Flaminio)
buildings.summary: A small temple of Pietas that Pliny says stood on the site later taken by the Theatre of Marcellus; Caesar demolished it with other shrines when he cleared the ground for his theatre.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 290
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Pietas, aedes in circo Flaminio
buildings.note: Location only known as 'where the Theatre of Marcellus is'; placed under the stage area. Form invented from typical small Republican temples.

buildings.name: Theatre of Marcellus
buildings.builderName: begun by Julius Caesar, completed by Augustus
buildings.summary: Begun by Caesar, who demolished temples to clear the site, and finished by Augustus in the name of his dead nephew and heir Marcellus; dedicated in 13 or 11 BC. A travertine cavea about 111 m across with three tiers of arcades (Doric, Ionic and a Corinthian attic) rising 32.6 m, seating perhaps 15,000. Its stage looked toward the Tiber.

phases.t: used, perhaps unfinished, for the scenic games of the Secular Games
dedicated in the name of Marcellus (Dio; Pliny gives 11 BC)

scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 382-383
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
Fidenzoni, Il teatro di Marcello (1970)
Ciancio Rossetto, in LTUR V (1999)
buildings.note: Centre fitted to the surviving curve of the facade (radius ~56 m). The curved facade wraps the north and east, so the audience looked WSW toward the stage on the river side; rot 258 is estimated from the arc and could be off by 10 degrees. Height 32.6 m to the top of the attic. Dio dates the dedication to 13 BC, Pliny to 11 BC.

buildings.name: Theatre of Marcellus (Flavian and Severan restorations)
buildings.summary: Vespasian restored the stage building and Severus Alexander repaired the theatre again; it remained one of the three great stone theatres of Rome through the 4th century.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 383
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Theatrum Marcelli
buildings.note: Same form; restoration dates approximate.

buildings.name: Theatre of Marcellus (late antique)
buildings.summary: Travertine blocks were taken from the theatre around 370 to rebuild the Pons Cestius as the Pons Gratiani, a sign that parts of it were already derelict; yet in 421 the prefect Petronius Maximus still set up statues here. After the 6th century it decayed into a quarry and later a fortress of the Pierleoni, Savelli and Orsini.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 383
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Theatrum Marcelli
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
buildings.note: The Ammianus passage concerns the prefect Symmachus and the bridge; the reuse of the theatre's travertine for the Pons Gratiani is inferred by modern scholars. Statues of Petronius Maximus are known from inscriptions. Stage height reduced to show partial dismantling.

buildings.name: Porticus Metelli
buildings.summary: Built by Q. Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus after his Macedonian triumph of 146 BC around the temples of Jupiter Stator and Juno Regina. In front of the temples stood Lysippus' bronze group of Alexander's 25 horsemen at the Granicus, taken as booty from Dion in Macedonia.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 317
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Porticus Metelli
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project (formaurbis.stanford.edu), fr. 31u
buildings.note: Assumed to share the later footprint (Marble Plan shows the Severan state about 119 x 132 m). Facade (and the surviving propylon) faces SW onto the Circus Flaminius; rot 214 from the alignment of the propylon and Via del Portico d'Ottavia.

buildings.name: Porticus Octaviae (Augustan)
buildings.summary: Augustus rebuilt the porticus in his sister Octavia's name, adding a library (Latin and Greek, founded by Octavia in memory of Marcellus), a curia and scholae, and filling it with Greek art: works by Praxiteles, Phidias, Apelles and others. The Senate sometimes met in its curia.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 317-318
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Porticus Octaviae
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (JRA Suppl. 50, 2002)
buildings.note: Dio (49.43.8) dates a dedication to 33 BC, perhaps confusing it with the Porticus Octavia of Cn. Octavius; work is usually placed after 27 BC (from = -23 as a mid-range date).

buildings.name: Porticus Octaviae (Domitianic)
buildings.summary: The fire of AD 80 destroyed Octavia's buildings and their books (Dio). They were restored, probably under Domitian.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 318
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Porticus Octaviae
buildings.note: Restoration by Domitian is likely but not attested by inscription.

buildings.name: Porticus Octaviae (Severan)
buildings.summary: After a fire (that of 191) Septimius Severus and Caracalla restored the porticus in 203, as the inscription on the surviving propylon records. The Marble Plan, made in these same years, shows it with its two temples and double colonnades.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 318
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project (formaurbis.stanford.edu), fr. 31u, 31bb
buildings.note: Propylon remains: brick-faced concrete and marble, four columns across the front; dedicatory inscription of 203 on the architrave.

buildings.name: Porticus Octaviae (after the earthquake of 442)
buildings.summary: Two columns of the propylon's front, brought down by the earthquake of 442, were replaced with the brick arch still visible. The porticus became the medieval fish market and the church of Sant'Angelo in Pescheria was built into the propylon in 755.
scholarship: Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Porticus Octaviae
buildings.note: The arch is generally attributed to the repair after the earthquake of 442.

buildings.name: Temple of Jupiter Stator (Porticus Metelli)
buildings.summary: The first temple in Rome built entirely of marble, designed by the Greek architect Hermodoros of Salamis for Metellus Macedonicus. Vitruvius cites it as the model peripteros, six columns by eleven.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 225
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Iuppiter Stator, aedes in circo
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project (formaurbis.stanford.edu), fr. 31u
buildings.note: Position inside the porticus from the Marble Plan: the two temples stand side by side facing the propylon, Jupiter to the south. Order uncertain (Ionic assumed for a Hermodoran temple).

buildings.name: Temple of Jupiter Stator (Domitianic)
buildings.summary: Restored after the fire of 80 with the rest of the porticus.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 225
buildings.note: Form as v1.

buildings.name: Temple of Jupiter Stator (Severan)
buildings.summary: Rebuilt with the porticus by Septimius Severus and Caracalla in 203; shown on the Marble Plan.

Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 225

buildings.name: Temple of Juno Regina (in campo)
buildings.summary: Vowed by M. Aemilius Lepidus in the Ligurian war of 187 BC and dedicated by him as censor on 23 December 179; later enclosed with Jupiter Stator in the Porticus Metelli.

buildings.name: Temple of Juno Regina (Domitianic)
buildings.summary: Restored after the fire of 80.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 216

buildings.name: Temple of Juno Regina (Severan)
buildings.summary: Rebuilt in 203 with the porticus; columns of its pronaos survive built into houses on Via di Sant'Angelo in Pescheria.

buildings.name: Porticus Philippi
buildings.summary: L. Marcius Philippus, Augustus' stepfather, rebuilt the Temple of Hercules Musarum and enclosed it in this porticus about 29 BC, part of the Augustan transformation of the Circus Flaminius. It held paintings by Zeuxis, Antiphilus and Theon and became a haunt of Rome's poets and hairdressers alike.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 318-319
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Porticus Philippi

buildings.note: Immediately WNW of the Porticus Octaviae, sharing its alignment and facade line onto the Circus (Marble Plan). Depth reduced to 96 m so as not to collide with the Theatre of Balbus; true depth unknown.

buildings.name: Porticus Philippi (Severan)
buildings.summary: Shown on the Severan Marble Plan beside the Porticus Octaviae; restored with its neighbour after the fire of 191 (assumed).
scholarship: Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project (formaurbis.stanford.edu), fr. 31u, 31cc
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 319

buildings.name: Temple of Hercules Musarum
buildings.summary: Built by M. Fulvius Nobilior from the spoils of Ambracia (189 BC), where he took the statues of the nine Muses and of Hercules playing the lyre; the poet Ennius had accompanied him. Fulvius also set up here the Fasti, a calendar with commentary.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 187
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Hercules Musarum, aedes
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project (formaurbis.stanford.edu), fr. 31u

buildings.name: Temple of Hercules Musarum (rebuilt by Philippus)
buildings.summary: Rebuilt by L. Marcius Philippus within his new porticus; shown on the Marble Plan as a rotunda with porch.

Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 187

buildings.name: Porticus Octavia (of Cn. Octavius)
buildings.summary: A double porticus built by Gn. Octavius after his naval triumph over Perseus in 167 BC, famous for its bronze Corinthian capitals, hence 'Corinthia'. It stood near the Circus Flaminius.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 317
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Porticus Octavia
buildings.note: Location unknown beyond 'near the Circus Flaminius'; placed WNW of the Porticus Philippi on the same facade line. Size invented.

buildings.name: Porticus Octavia (rebuilt by Octavian)
buildings.summary: Octavian rebuilt it in 33 BC with the spoils of his Illyrian war, keeping the name of its founder, and placed there the standards recovered from the Dalmatians.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 317
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (JRA Suppl. 50, 2002)

buildings.name: Temple of Neptune (in circo Flaminio)
buildings.summary: A temple of Neptune 'in circo Flaminio' is attested by 206 BC, when it sweated as a prodigy.

Coarelli, Il Campo Marzio dalle origini alla fine della repubblica (1997)

buildings.name: Temple of Neptune (Gn. Domitius Ahenobarbus)
buildings.summary: Rebuilt by Gn. Domitius Ahenobarbus, Antony's admiral, perhaps around 32 BC, with Scopas' great marine group of Neptune, Thetis, Achilles and Nereids. The 'Altar of Domitius Ahenobarbus' reliefs (census scene and marine thiasos, now in Paris and Munich) probably belonged to its statue base. Burned in 80 and restored.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 267

buildings.name: Temple of Mars (in circo Flaminio)
buildings.summary: Built by D. Junius Brutus Callaicus from his Spanish spoils of 138-133 BC, designed by Hermodoros of Salamis, with a colossal seated Mars and a nude Venus by Scopas Minor; the triumphator inscribed verses by the poet Accius at its entrance.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 245
Coarelli, Il Campo Marzio dalle origini alla fine della repubblica (1997)

buildings.name: Temple of Castor and Pollux (in circo Flaminio)
buildings.summary: A temple of the Dioscuri 'in circo Flaminio', described by Vitruvius as an example of a temple with the cella set transversely, wider than deep, like the Temple of Veiovis. A fragment of a marble plan (the 'Via Anicia' plan) shows it beside the river.

buildings.name: Temple of Hercules Magnus Custos
buildings.summary: The temple of Hercules the Guardian at the end of the Circus Flaminius, said by Ovid to have been approved by the Sibylline Books; restored by Sulla.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 186
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Hercules Magnus Custos
buildings.note: Ovid places it at one end of the Circus ('altera pars circi'); the ESE end is taken by the Theatre of Marcellus in our model, so it is set on the north side toward the WNW end, facing the Circus. Position, date (Hannibalic war) and form are conjectural.

buildings.name: Amphitheatre of Statilius Taurus
buildings.summary: Rome's first permanent amphitheatre, built in stone (partly) by Augustus' general T. Statilius Taurus and opened with games in 29 BC; Caligula found it too modest. It burned in the Great Fire of 64 and was not rebuilt.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 11

buildings.name: Temple B (Fortuna Huiusce Diei)
buildings.summary: A round temple ringed by 18 columns, vowed by Q. Lutatius Catulus at the battle of Vercellae against the Cimbri in 101 BC to the Fortune of This Very Day. Its cult statue was a colossal acrolith by Skopas Minor (?), whose head and arm survive (Centrale Montemartini). Six columns stand.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

buildings.note: Diameter of the colonnade about 19 m; column height ~11 m estimated from the surviving tufa columns. The cella stood free inside the colonnade in this phase.

buildings.name: Temple B (enlarged cella)
buildings.summary: In a second Republican phase the intercolumniations were walled up to enlarge the cella and the podium and front stair were extended.

buildings.name: Temple B (Domitianic)
buildings.summary: Restored after the fire of 80 at the level of the new travertine pavement.

buildings.name: Temple D (Lares Permarini?)
buildings.summary: The largest of the four, mostly still under Via Florida. Probably the temple of the Lares Permarini, the guardians of seafarers, vowed by L. Aemilius Regillus in the naval battle against Antiochus' fleet in 190 BC and dedicated by M. Aemilius Lepidus as censor on 22 December 179, 'in porticu Minucia'.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)

buildings.note: Identification follows Coarelli (the Fasti Praenestini place the Lares Permarini in the Porticus Minucia). Only the northern part is excavated; size about 40 x 22 m.

buildings.name: Temple D (late Republican travertine rebuilding)
buildings.summary: Rebuilt in travertine in the late Republic.

buildings.name: Temple D (Domitianic)
buildings.summary: Restored after the fire of 80 with brick-faced walls.

buildings.name: Great latrine of the Area Sacra
buildings.summary: A large public latrine built behind Temples A and B against the Hecatostylum in the imperial period.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)

buildings.name: Porticus Minucia Vetus
buildings.summary: Built by M. Minucius Rufus from the spoils of his Thracian victory (triumph 106 BC). In Coarelli's interpretation it enclosed the four Largo Argentina temples, Temple D being described as 'in porticu Minucia'.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 315
Coarelli, Il Campo Marzio dalle origini alla fine della repubblica (1997)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Porticus Minucia vetus
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project (formaurbis.stanford.edu)
buildings.note: Debated. Coarelli: around the Area Sacra di Largo Argentina (followed here). Others (Manacorda, Rodriguez-Almeida) put the Minucia at Via delle Botteghe Oscure. sides: n = front (east), e = right (south), w = left (north); the back (west) is closed by the Porticus of Pompey and its Curia.

buildings.name: Porticus Minucia Vetus (Domitianic)
buildings.summary: Rebuilt with the Area Sacra after the fire of 80.
scholarship: Coarelli, Il Campo Marzio dalle origini alla fine della repubblica (1997)
buildings.note: As v1.

buildings.name: Porticus Minucia Frumentaria
buildings.summary: The seat of the monthly free grain distribution to the plebs, where citizens presented their tesserae at one of 45 numbered entrances (ostia); it existed by the reign of Claudius.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 315-316
Coarelli, Il Campo Marzio dalle origini alla fine della repubblica (1997)

buildings.note: Coarelli puts it immediately east of the Crypta Balbi around the temple at Via delle Botteghe Oscure. Size (about 100 m square) and date are conjectural.

buildings.name: Temple of the Nymphs (Aedes Nympharum)
buildings.summary: Where the censors' records were kept. Clodius' gangs burned it in 57 BC to destroy the census records, as Cicero repeatedly charged.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 268
Coarelli, Il Campo Marzio dalle origini alla fine della repubblica (1997)
Manacorda, Crypta Balbi (2001)
buildings.note: Identified by Coarelli with the temple remains under Via delle Botteghe Oscure, later inside the Porticus Minucia Frumentaria. Date of founding unknown (179 BC assumed, with Lepidus' censorship); orientation guessed.

buildings.name: Temple of the Nymphs (rebuilt)
buildings.summary: Rebuilt after Clodius' arson; the visible podium under Via delle Botteghe Oscure belongs to a late Republican phase.
scholarship: Coarelli, Il Campo Marzio dalle origini alla fine della repubblica (1997)
buildings.note: As v1.

buildings.name: Villa Publica
buildings.summary: Built by the censors of 435 BC as the base of the census and the levy, an official residence in an enclosed park where generals awaiting a triumph and foreign envoys could stay outside the pomerium.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 430
Coarelli, Il Campo Marzio dalle origini alla fine della repubblica (1997)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Villa Publica
buildings.note: Location debated: south of the Saepta, on the later site of the Divorum (followed here, Richardson) or at Via delle Botteghe Oscure. Form invented: a walled park with a modest courtyard house.

buildings.name: Villa Publica (rebuilt 194 BC)
buildings.summary: Rebuilt and enlarged by the censors of 194 BC; a coin of 59 BC shows a two-storey colonnaded building. Sulla had 6,000 prisoners massacred here in 82 BC within earshot of the Senate, and Varro set his dialogue on farming here. It disappeared under Domitian's Divorum after the fire of 80.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 430
Coarelli, Il Campo Marzio dalle origini alla fine della repubblica (1997)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Villa Publica
buildings.note: As v1.

buildings.name: Saepta (Ovile), Republican voting enclosure
buildings.summary: The wooden pens (the 'sheepfold') in which the centuries of the comitia centuriata were marshalled to vote in the Campus Martius, replaced by Caesar's and Agrippa's marble Saepta.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 340
Coarelli, Il Campo Marzio dalle origini alla fine della repubblica (1997)
buildings.note: Assumed to have occupied roughly the site of the later Saepta Julia; form and start date invented.

buildings.name: Altar of Mars (Ara Martis in Campo)
buildings.summary: The ancient altar of Mars that gave the Campus its name, where the censors performed the lustrum that closed the census. It stood near the Villa Publica.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 245
Coarelli, Il Campo Marzio dalle origini alla fine della repubblica (1997)
buildings.note: Location near the Villa Publica per Livy; exact spot unknown.

buildings.name: Theatre of Pompey
buildings.summary: Rome's first permanent stone theatre, dedicated by Pompey in his second consulship in 55 BC with games in which 500 lions and 18 elephants died. To evade the old ban on permanent theatres, a temple of Venus Victrix crowned the top of the cavea so that the seats served as its steps; the temple was dedicated in 52. The cavea was about 150 m across.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 383-385
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)

Gagliardo and Packer, 'A new look at Pompey's theater', AJA 110 (2006)
Stanford Digital Forma Urbis Romae Project (formaurbis.stanford.edu), fr. 39
buildings.note: Cavea centre fitted to the curve of Via di Grotta Pinta, which follows the inner cavea; the outer edge reaches the houses of Piazza del Biscione. The stage faced east toward the porticus: rot 92 (audience looks slightly south of east), consistent with the Curia Pompeia ~200 m away on the same axis. Height ~45 m to the temple roof (estimate). Seat count of 17,500 is the Regionary figure divided; ancient numbers vary (Pliny 40,000).

buildings.name: Theatre of Pompey (Augustan restoration)
buildings.summary: Augustus restored the theatre at great expense in 32 BC without adding his own name, and placed Pompey's statue, removed from the Curia, on a marble arch facing the theatre's royal door.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 383-385

buildings.name: Theatre of Pompey (Tiberian-Claudian rebuilding)
buildings.summary: Burned in AD 22; Tiberius began the rebuilding, Caligula continued it and Claudius rededicated it in Pompey's name. Nero had it gilded inside and out for one day for the visit of Tiridates of Armenia in 66.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 383-385
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)

buildings.note: Form as before; the fire mostly damaged the scaena.

buildings.name: Theatre of Pompey (Flavian to Diocletianic)
buildings.summary: The scaena burned again in AD 80 and was restored; Septimius Severus repaired it, and Diocletian and Maximian restored the theatre after the fire of 283. It remained in use for spectacles into the 5th century.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 383-385

buildings.name: Theatre of Pompey (Theodoric's restoration)
buildings.summary: Theodoric commissioned the senator Symmachus to restore the theatre, whose great vaults were threatening collapse; his letter marvels at the 'caves' of the cavea. After the Gothic wars it fell slowly into ruin and was built over in the Middle Ages, its curve preserved by the houses of Via di Grotta Pinta.

buildings.name: Porticus of Pompey
buildings.summary: The great quadriporticus behind the stage of Pompey's theatre, about 180 x 135 m, planted with double rows of plane trees and fountains, hung with paintings and tapestries and full of statues: the favourite promenade of Rome, where Catullus hunted for his friend and Ovid sent lovers looking. At its far (east) end stood the Curia of Pompey.

buildings.summary: The porticus and the Hecatostylum burned under Philip the Arab.

buildings.summary: Diocletian and Maximian rebuilt the twin porticoes, renamed Porticus Iovia and Porticus Herculia after their divine patrons; the Regionary Catalogues list 'Porticus II'.

buildings.name: Curia of Pompey
buildings.summary: The hall at the east end of the porticus where the Senate met while the Curia Hostilia was being rebuilt. Here on the Ides of March 44 BC Caesar was stabbed 23 times and fell at the foot of Pompey's statue. Its tufa platform lies behind Temples B and C of Largo Argentina.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 104
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)

buildings.note: Faces west (rot 272) into the porticus; its back wall abutted the temples. Dimensions approximate from the excavated platform (about 25 m wide).

buildings.name: Curia of Pompey (walled up)
buildings.summary: After the murder the Senate declared the place accursed and had it walled up; Augustus moved Pompey's statue to a marble arch facing the theatre. In the imperial period a concrete structure, perhaps a memorial, was built in the closed hall.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 104
Coarelli, Il Foro Romano II (1985)

buildings.name: Hecatostylum (Porch of a Hundred Columns)
buildings.summary: A long colonnade of a hundred columns along the north side of the Pompeian complex and the Area Sacra, shown on the Marble Plan; Martial calls it the 'hundred columns'.

buildings.name: Hecatostylum (burned)

buildings.name: Temple of Fortuna Equestris
buildings.summary: Vowed by Q. Fulvius Flaccus in a cavalry battle in Spain in 180 BC and dedicated in 173; he scandalously stripped the marble roof tiles from the temple of Juno Lacinia at Croton for it and was made to return them. Vitruvius saw it 'by the stone theatre'; by AD 22 it no longer existed.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 154

buildings.note: Location 'ad theatrum lapideum' (Vitruvius); placed just north of the cavea of Pompey's theatre. Disappearance date between Vitruvius and AD 22 (to = 10 arbitrary).

buildings.name: Theatre of Balbus
buildings.summary: The smallest of Rome's three stone theatres, built by L. Cornelius Balbus the Younger from the spoils of his African triumph (19 BC) and dedicated in 13 BC, when the Tiber was in flood and Balbus could reach it only by boat. Its stage boasted four small columns of onyx.

buildings.name: Theatre of Balbus (restored after 80)
buildings.summary: Burned in 80 and restored; still listed in the Regionary Catalogues of the 4th century.
